'''Don Nelson Page''' {{postnominals|country=CAN|FRSC}} (born December 31, 1948) is an American-born Canadian theoretical [[physicist]] at the [[University of Alberta]], Canada.<ref name="physics.ualberta.ca">{{cite web|url=http://www.physics.ualberta.ca/Faculty/DonPage |title=Don Page - University of Alberta |access-date=2013-09-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130927081556/http://www.physics.ualberta.ca/Faculty/DonPage |archive-date=2013-09-27 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.jewell.edu/gen/media/achieve/fall2005/foundInTheCosmos.html |title=Achieve Magazine |access-date=2015-02-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150213030724/http://www.jewell.edu/gen/media/achieve/fall2005/foundInTheCosmos.html |archive-date=2015-02-13 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AZxPAQAAIAAJ|title=Reports ... John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation|last=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation|date=Jun 24, 1986|publisher=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation.|access-date=Jun 24, 2020|via=Google Books}}</ref>

==Work==
Page's work focuses on [[quantum cosmology]] and theoretical gravitational physics, and he is noted for being a doctoral student of [[Stephen Hawking]], who was at [[Caltech]] during 1974-1975, in addition to publishing several journal articles with him.<ref>{{cite Q|Q59348104}}</ref><ref>{{cite Q|Q59348141}}</ref> 
Page got his BA at [[William Jewell College]] in the United States in 1971, attaining an MS in 1972 and a PhD in 1976 at [[Caltech]].<ref name="thesis-page-1976">{{cite thesis |url=https://thesis.library.caltech.edu/7179/ |title=Accretion into and emission from black holes. |date=1976 |publisher=[[California Institute of Technology]] |type=Ph.D. |last=Page |first=Don Nelson |oclc=945995991}}</ref>

His professional career started as a research assistant in Cambridge from 1976-1979, followed by an assistant professorship at [[Penn State]] from 1979-1983, and then an associate professor at Penn State until 1986 before taking on the title of professor in 1986. Page spent four more years at Penn State before moving to become a professor at the [[University of Alberta]] in Canada in 1990.

In 1993, he argued that if a [[black hole]] starts in a pure quantum state and evaporates completely by a [[unitarity (physics)|unitary process]], the [[von Neumann entropy]] of the [[Hawking radiation]] initially increases and then decreases back to zero when the black hole has disappeared.<ref name="1993-page">{{cite journal | volume=71 | last = Page | first = Don N. | title = Information in Black Hole Radiation | journal = Physical Review Letters | pages = 3743–3746 | date = 6 December 1993 | issue = 23 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.71.3743 | arxiv=hep-th/9306083 |bibcode = 1993PhRvL..71.3743P | pmid = 10055062 | s2cid = 9363821 }}</ref> This is known as the Page curve, and the turnover point of the curve the Page time.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Almheiri |first1=Ahmed |last2=Hartman |first2=Thomas |last3=Maldacena |first3=Juan |author-link3=Juan Maldacena |last4=Shaghoulian |first4=Edgar |last5=Tajdini |first5=Amirhossein |title=The entropy of Hawking radiation |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |date=21 July 2021 |volume=93 |issue=3 |article-number=035002 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.93.035002|arxiv=2006.06872 |bibcode=2021RvMP...93c5002A |s2cid=219635921 |quote=Glossary. Page curve: Consider a spacetime with a black hole formed by the collapse of a pure state. Surround the black hole by an imaginary sphere whose radius is a few Schwarzschild radii. The Page curve is a plot of the fine-grained entropy outside of this imaginary sphere, where we subtract the contribution of the vacuum. Since the black hole Hawking radiates and the Hawking quanta enter this faraway region, this computes the fine-grained entropy of Hawking radiation as a function of time. Notice that the regions inside and outside the imaginary sphere are open systems. The curve begins at zero when no Hawking quanta have entered the exterior region, and ends at zero when the black hole has completely evaporated and all of the Hawking quanta are in the exterior region. The "Page time" corresponds to the turnover point of the curve. }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Cox |first1=Brian |last2=Forshaw |first2=Jeff |title=Black Holes: the key to understanding the Universe |date=2022 |publisher=HarperCollins Publishers |location=New York, NY |isbn=978-0-06-293669-1 |pages=220–225}}</ref> For many researchers, deriving the Page curve is synonymous with solving the famous [[black hole information paradox]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Grumiller |first1=Daniel |last2=Sheikh-Jabbari |first2=Mohammad Mehdi |title=Black Hole Physics: From Collapse to Evaporation |date=2022 |publisher=Springer Graduate Texts in Physics |location=Switzerland |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-10343-8 |isbn=978-3-031-10342-1 |s2cid=253372811 |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-031-10343-8}}</ref>{{rp|291}}

==Awards and honors==
In 2012, Page became a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.ualberta.ca/science/about-us/contours/2012-winter-contours/2012/january/physicist-don-page-named-to-the-royal-society-of-canada |title=Physicist Don Page named to the Royal Society of Canada |date=January 20, 2012 |work=[[University of Alberta]] |access-date=March 24, 2018 |archive-date=November 26, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181126202631/https://www.ualberta.ca/science/about-us/contours/2012-winter-contours/2012/january/physicist-don-page-named-to-the-royal-society-of-canada }}</ref>

==Religious views==
Page is an [[Evangelicalism|Evangelical Christian]]. In commenting on the debate between [[William Lane Craig]] and [[Sean M. Carroll|Sean Carroll]] in 2014, he states in a guest post on Carroll's website that: "...in view of all the evidence, including both the elegance of the laws of physics, the existence of orderly sentient experiences, and the historical evidence, I do believe that [[God]] exists and think the world is actually simpler if it contains God than it would have been without God."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.preposterousuniverse.com/blog/2015/03/20/guest-post-don-page-on-god-and-cosmology/ | title=Guest Post: Don Page on God and Cosmology | date=March 20, 2015 |access-date=August 28, 2019}}</ref> In the same post he criticises William Lane Craig's [[Kalam Cosmological Argument]], saying that it "is highly dubious metaphysically, depending on contingent intuitions [i.e. the first premise] we have developed from living in a universe with relatively simple laws of physics and with a strong thermodynamic arrow of time."
